# SK1041 — Use a compound assignment

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An assignment whose right-hand side is a binary operation on the assignment target itself, where the compound operator says it once.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

Naming the target twice is the shape a rename can half-finish: `total = subtotal + 1` compiles and is a different program, and nothing in the long form says which of the two occurrences was meant. The compound form cannot drift, and it is the form C# has had since version 1 — the long one is what a model writes because most of its training data predates the habit.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
count = count + 1;
```

Write:

```csharp
count += 1;
```

## When it does not fire

The direction is safe and the reverse is not: C# defines `x op= y` as `x = (T)(x op y)` with an explicit conversion back to the target's type, which the long form lacks — `byte b; b = b + 1;` does not compile at all, so the rule never sees the shapes where the conversion differs. A cast on the right-hand side is therefore never unwrapped: `long l; l = (int)(l + 1);` truncates and `l += 1` does not. Only whole expression statements are reported, the target must be a chain of plain names so that the two forms evaluate it the same number of times, and the binary operator's left operand must be that same target textually — which excludes `x = x + a + b`, whose left operand is `x + a`. `&&` and `||` have no compound spelling and are excluded. Comments and preprocessor directives between the target and the operator are excluded because the fix deletes that text.

## Configuration

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK1041.severity`
